questions.stem: The cell theory has been modified as new evidence emerged. Which observation supports the idea that cells arise only from pre-existing cells?
options: Under a microscope, new cells are seen forming only when existing cells divide
Sealed flasks of boiled broth produce new cells within a few hours of being cooled
Viruses can be seen assembling themselves from proteins outside any cell
Cells can be made in a laboratory by mixing lipids, sugars and amino acids
questions.explanation: Observations of cell division, and experiments showing sterile sealed broth stays free of microbes, support the principle that cells come only from pre-existing cells. No one has made a living cell by mixing its chemical components.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane?
options: A phospholipid bilayer in which proteins are scattered and can move sideways
A rigid layer of protein sandwiched between two fixed layers of phospholipid
A single layer of phospholipids with all proteins attached on the outside
A network of cellulose fibres with lipid droplets set between the fibres
questions.explanation: The membrane is a bilayer of phospholipids that can move laterally (fluid), with a mosaic of proteins embedded in it or attached to its surfaces. The older protein-lipid-protein sandwich model was replaced by this one.

questions.stem: In the phospholipid bilayer, how are the phospholipid molecules arranged?
options: Heads and tails alternate at random so that water can pass straight through
Hydrophilic heads face the water on each side; hydrophobic tails face inwards
Hydrophobic tails face the water on each side; hydrophilic heads face inwards
All heads face the cytoplasm, and all tails face the outside of the cell
questions.explanation: Phosphate heads are attracted to water, so they face the watery cytoplasm and tissue fluid, while the fatty acid tails avoid water and form the membrane's interior. This hydrophobic core restricts the passage of ions and polar molecules.

questions.stem: Oxygen and steroid hormones cross the membrane easily, but glucose and sodium ions need membrane proteins to cross. What property of the bilayer explains this?
options: Its proteins carry oxygen and steroids, while glucose and ions dissolve in the lipid
Its hydrophobic interior lets small non-polar and lipid-soluble molecules through but blocks charged and polar ones
Its hydrophilic interior lets charged and polar molecules through but blocks small non-polar and lipid-soluble ones
Its pores are large enough for glucose and ions but too small for oxygen and steroids
questions.explanation: The fatty acid tails form a non-polar core, so oxygen and lipid-soluble molecules such as steroids dissolve through it. Ions and polar molecules like glucose are repelled by the core and need channel or carrier proteins.

questions.stem: Which statement about prokaryotes is correct?
options: They have chromosomes inside a nucleus
They are larger than most plant cells
They exist only as single cells
They form tissues in large organisms
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes, bacteria and archaea, only exist as single cells, although some live in colonies. They have no nucleus, and they are usually much smaller than eukaryotic cells.

questions.stem: Which row correctly compares a bacterial cell with a eukaryotic cell?
options: Prokaryotic chromosomes: linear, in a nucleus; eukaryotic: circular, in the cytosol
Prokaryotic cells: 10 to 100 micrometres; eukaryotic cells: 1 to 10 micrometres
Prokaryotic cells: many organelles; eukaryotic cells: no internal membranes at all
Prokaryotic chromosome: circular, in the cytosol; eukaryotic: linear, in a nucleus
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes usually have one circular chromosome in the cytosol, are typically about 1 to 10 micrometres across, and lack membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes have linear chromosomes in a nucleus and internal membranes.

questions.stem: A cell is 3 micrometres long, has ribosomes, a cell wall and a single circular chromosome, and no internal membranes. Why does it carry out respiration on its cell membrane rather than in mitochondria?
options: It is a plant cell, so its chloroplasts replace mitochondria in respiration
It is a fungal cell, so all of its respiration happens inside the ribosomes
It is a prokaryote, so it has no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria
It is a eukaryote that has lost its mitochondria by moving them to the cell wall
questions.explanation: Small size, a circular chromosome and no internal membranes identify a prokaryote. Lacking mitochondria, prokaryotes carry out the membrane-based steps of aerobic respiration on their cell membrane.

questions.stem: What is the function of the nucleolus?
options: Packaging proteins into vesicles for export from the cell
Breaking down worn-out organelles using digestive enzymes
Making ribosomal RNA and assembling ribosome subunits
Storing the cell's supply of glucose as starch grains
questions.explanation: The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus where rRNA is made and combined with proteins to form ribosome subunits. Packaging proteins is the job of the Golgi body, and digestion is done by lysosomes.

questions.stem: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration in eukaryotic cells?
options: Golgi body
Nucleolus
Mitochondrion
Chloroplast
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out the aerobic stages of cellular respiration, producing most of the cell's ATP. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
options: It stores water and keeps plant cells firm by turgor
It captures light energy and converts it to chemical energy
Its ribosomes make proteins that are transported in vesicles
It makes lipids and breaks down toxins such as alcohol in the cell
questions.explanation: Rough ER is studded with ribosomes that make proteins for membranes, lysosomes or export, which then travel in vesicles to the Golgi body. Smooth ER, without ribosomes, makes lipids and detoxifies substances.

questions.stem: What does the Golgi body do with proteins it receives from the endoplasmic reticulum?
options: Copies them so that each daughter cell has some
Modifies, sorts and packages them into vesicles
Translates them from mRNA into new amino acids
Breaks them down into amino acids for energy
questions.explanation: The Golgi body modifies proteins, for example by adding carbohydrates, then sorts and packages them into vesicles that go to the cell membrane for secretion or to other organelles. Proteins are made at ribosomes, not in the Golgi.

questions.stem: Cells of the pancreas secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes. Which pathway do these enzymes follow from synthesis to release?
options: Smooth ER, mitochondrion, vesicle, Golgi body, diffusion through the membrane
Nucleus, lysosome, Golgi body, ribosome, active transport through a channel
Rough ER, vesicle, Golgi body, vesicle, exocytosis at the cell membrane
Golgi body, nucleolus, rough ER, lysosome, endocytosis at the membrane
questions.explanation: Secreted proteins are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, carried in vesicles to the Golgi body for modification and packaging, then carried in vesicles that fuse with the membrane to release them by exocytosis.

questions.stem: Which statement describes lysosomes?
options: Double-membraned organelles that make ATP using oxygen and glucose from the blood
Stacks of flattened sacs that modify proteins and package them for secretion
Small structures of RNA and protein that build new polypeptides from single amino acids
Membrane-bound sacs of enzymes that digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material
questions.explanation: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and material taken in by endocytosis, such as bacteria engulfed by phagocytes. The other descriptions fit mitochondria, the Golgi body and ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which is a function of the cytoskeleton?
options: Producing glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy
Maintaining cell shape and moving organelles and vesicles within the cell
Controlling which of the substances enter and leave the cell at its outer surface
Storing the genetic information that controls the cell's activities
questions.explanation: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments and microtubules that supports the cell, helps it change shape and move, guides vesicles and organelles, and forms the spindle in cell division.

questions.stem: Which feature of the large central vacuole is important in a plant cell?
options: It contains chlorophyll and carries out most of the photosynthesis in a leaf
It makes the cellulose that strengthens the cell wall from outside
It stores water and solutes, keeping the cell firm by pressing on the wall
It contains the chromosomes and controls the activities of the cell
questions.explanation: The large vacuole holds cell sap. When it is full of water it presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall, making the cell turgid and supporting non-woody plants. Chromosomes are in the nucleus and chlorophyll is in chloroplasts.

questions.stem: A biologist finds that cells from a gland have very large amounts of smooth ER. Which function is this gland most likely to have?
options: Absorbing light to make glucose for the body
Storing starch grains for later energy use
Producing and secreting steroid (lipid) hormones
Producing and secreting large digestive protein enzymes
questions.explanation: Smooth ER makes lipids, including steroid hormones, so glands that secrete steroids such as those in the adrenal cortex have a lot of it. Cells secreting protein enzymes have abundant rough ER instead.

questions.stem: Why is the folding of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion into cristae an advantage?
options: It allows the mitochondrion to divide more quickly than the cell does
It stores glucose between the folds until the cell needs to use it
It increases the surface area for the membrane-bound enzymes that make ATP
It reduces the surface area so that fewer enzymes are needed for respiration
questions.explanation: Many reactions of aerobic respiration take place on the inner membrane, so folding it into cristae provides more surface area for the enzymes and proteins involved, increasing ATP production.

questions.stem: Which structures are found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
options: A nucleus, a Golgi body and the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes, a cytoskeleton and many small vesicles
A cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole
A cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and usually a large central vacuole. Both plant and animal cells have a membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER and Golgi.

questions.stem: How does a fungal cell differ from a plant cell?
options: It has no cell wall and contains many chloroplasts
It has no nucleus and a single circular chromosome
It has a cellulose wall and one large central vacuole for storage
It has a cell wall made of chitin and no chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Fungal cells are eukaryotic with a cell wall, but the wall is made of chitin rather than cellulose, and they have no chloroplasts, so fungi are heterotrophs.

questions.stem: An electron micrograph shows a cell with a nucleus, mitochondria, a cell wall and no chloroplasts. Which conclusion is most secure?
options: It must be a leaf cell, because all cells with walls are found in leaves
It is a eukaryotic cell, possibly fungal or from a non-green part of a plant
It must be a bacterial cell, because it has a cell wall and has no chloroplasts at all
It must be an animal cell, because it has mitochondria and a nucleus
questions.explanation: A nucleus and mitochondria show it is eukaryotic, and a wall rules out an animal cell. A fungal cell or a plant cell from a root, which has no chloroplasts, both fit. Bacteria have no nucleus.

questions.stem: Which process moves glucose into a red blood cell, down its concentration gradient, through a specific protein, without using ATP?
options: Simple diffusion
Exocytosis
Facilitated diffusion
Active transport
questions.explanation: Movement down a gradient through a membrane protein, with no energy input, is facilitated diffusion. Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a gradient, and simple diffusion does not need a protein.

questions.stem: What is the role of aquaporins in a cell membrane?
options: They are carrier proteins that pump water against its gradient using ATP
They are receptors that bind hormones and pass a signal into the cell
They are enzymes that split water molecules to release oxygen gas
They are channel proteins that let water cross the membrane quickly
questions.explanation: Aquaporins are channel proteins that allow water molecules to move rapidly across the membrane by osmosis. Water still moves passively, down its gradient; aquaporins only increase the rate.

questions.stem: How do channel proteins differ from carrier proteins?
options: Channels are found only in plants; carriers are found only in animals
Channels form pores for passive flow; carriers change shape to move substances
Channels always use ATP; carriers never use any energy to move their substances across
Channels move only lipids; carriers move only water and dissolved gases
questions.explanation: Channel proteins form water-filled pores through which specific ions or molecules flow down their gradient. Carrier proteins bind a substance and change shape to move it, either passively (facilitated diffusion) or actively using ATP.

questions.stem: Cells take up a substance even when its concentration inside is ten times higher than outside. Uptake stops when a respiratory poison is added. Which process is involved?
options: Active transport by carrier proteins
Facilitated diffusion through channels
Osmosis through aquaporins in the membrane
Simple diffusion through the phospholipids
questions.explanation: Moving a substance against its concentration gradient requires energy from ATP, made in respiration, so uptake that stops when respiration is poisoned is active transport. Diffusion and osmosis only move substances down gradients.

questions.stem: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium by surrounding it with its membrane and forming a vesicle. What is this process called?
options: Exocytosis
Osmosis
Facilitated diffusion
Endocytosis
questions.explanation: Endocytosis takes large particles or fluid into the cell inside vesicles formed from the membrane; engulfing solid particles like bacteria is phagocytosis. Exocytosis is the reverse, releasing materials from vesicles.

questions.stem: Which statement about endocytosis and exocytosis is correct?
options: Both move only single small molecules through channels
Both happen only in prokaryotic cells with cell walls
Both use vesicles and require energy from the cell
Both are passive and need no energy from the cell
questions.explanation: Endocytosis and exocytosis move large particles or bulk materials in membrane-bound vesicles, and both need energy (ATP) to move the vesicles and reshape the membrane.

questions.stem: Plant cells are placed in a solution with a higher water concentration than their cytoplasm. What happens?
options: Water enters by osmosis and the cells become turgid
Water leaves by osmosis and the cells become plasmolysed
Solutes enter by osmosis and the cells burst open
Water enters by active transport and the walls swell
questions.explanation: Water moves by osmosis from the dilute solution into the cells. The cell wall resists further expansion, so the cells become firm (turgid) instead of bursting, unlike animal cells.

questions.stem: Potato cylinders are placed in sucrose solutions for 24 hours. Mass change: 0.0 M +8%, 0.2 M +2%, 0.4 M -4%, 0.6 M -9%. What is the best estimate of the solute concentration at which there is no net water movement?
options: About 0.40 M
About 0.60 M
About 0.27 M
About 0.10 M
questions.explanation: No net water movement means zero mass change. The change passes from +2% at 0.2 M to -4% at 0.4 M; zero is one third of the way, at about 0.2 + 0.067 = 0.27 M. This is interpolation between the two closest data points.

questions.stem: Which molecule would cross a phospholipid bilayer most quickly without any membrane protein?
options: Carbon dioxide
Glucose
Sodium ion
Starch
questions.explanation: Small, non-polar molecules such as carbon dioxide and oxygen diffuse rapidly through the hydrophobic core. Glucose is polar, sodium ions are charged and starch is far too large.

questions.stem: How does the steepness of a concentration gradient affect the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
options: The gradient has no effect on the rate of diffusion
A steeper gradient stops diffusion and starts osmosis
A steeper gradient gives a faster rate of diffusion
A steeper gradient gives a slower rate of diffusion
questions.explanation: The rate of diffusion increases with the difference in concentration across the membrane. Cells and organs often maintain steep gradients, for example by removing substances once they have crossed.

questions.stem: Two cube-shaped cells have sides of 10 micrometres and 20 micrometres. How does the SA:V ratio of the larger cell compare with that of the smaller cell?
options: It is eight times smaller
It is the same, as both are cubes
It is half as large
It is twice as large
questions.explanation: For a cube of side L, SA:V = 6L squared / L cubed = 6/L. The small cell has 6/10 = 0.6 and the large one 6/20 = 0.3, so doubling the side halves the ratio and reduces the efficiency of exchange per unit volume.

questions.stem: Some cells that absorb nutrients have a membrane folded into microvilli. Which statement explains the advantage?
options: Folding removes the phospholipids, so all substances can diffuse freely
More membrane area means more carrier and channel proteins, increasing uptake
Folding thickens the membrane, so substances cannot leak back out of the cell
Folding increases the cell's volume, so the SA:V ratio becomes much smaller
questions.explanation: Microvilli greatly increase the surface area of the membrane without much increase in volume, providing more room for transport proteins and more area for diffusion. This speeds the uptake of materials.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains how a substance's physical and chemical nature affects how it crosses a membrane?
options: All substances cross at the same rate because the membrane is fully permeable
Only substances dissolved in water can cross; lipid-soluble substances are blocked
Large or charged substances need proteins or vesicles; small non-polar ones diffuse through the bilayer
Large or charged substances diffuse through the bilayer; small non-polar ones need proteins or vesicles
questions.explanation: Size, charge, polarity and lipid solubility determine the route: small non-polar or lipid-soluble molecules pass through the bilayer, ions and polar molecules need channel or carrier proteins, and very large particles need endocytosis or exocytosis.

questions.stem: Which process is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution?
options: Active transport
Exocytosis
Endocytosis
Osmosis
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the net passive movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of higher water concentration (dilute) to lower water concentration (concentrated).

questions.stem: Why is it important that the composition of the cytoplasm is kept relatively constant?
options: A constant composition stops the cell from ever needing to take in materials
Changes in composition would turn the cell membrane into a cell wall
Only a constant composition allows the cell to copy all of its chromosomes before dividing
Enzymes need suitable conditions, such as pH and ion levels, to work properly
questions.explanation: Cell reactions are controlled by enzymes that need suitable pH, ion and water levels. By controlling exchange, the membrane keeps conditions within the range in which enzymes and other proteins work.

questions.stem: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis and is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Mitochondrion
Golgi body
Lysosome
Ribosome
questions.explanation: Ribosomes, made of rRNA and protein, translate mRNA into polypeptides. They are found in all cells because they are not membrane-bound; mitochondria, the Golgi body and lysosomes occur only in eukaryotes.
